picked.title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
picked.summary: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

picked.title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
picked.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.

picked.title: Correct Robots Before They Make Mistakes: Proactive Human-in-the-Loop Intervention via Preference Learning
picked.summary: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.

picked.title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions
picked.summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.

picked.title: LeRobot Release v0.7.0
picked.summary: Release Blog https://huggingface.co/blog/lerobot/lerobot-release-v070 lerobot-070-release.mp4 ⚠️ Breaking changes (v0.6.1 -> v0.7.0) v0.7.0 rebuilds installation, training, inference and the hardware layer. A few changes need your attention when upgrading: Installation On Linux, torch and torchvision now come from PyPI as CUDA 13 builds (NVIDIA driver 580.65 or newer); the cu128 index is gone. For older drivers, install torch from a CUDA 12 index first (see the installation guide). macOS needs 14+ (15+ for MPS). Pins moved: transformers 5.22, huggingface-hub>=1.31,<3 , motorbridge 0.5, datasets<6 , Pillow<14 , torchcodec<0.18 . Training Weights & Biases is replaced by Trackio (the training extra installs trackio ): --wandb.* is now --trackio.* , entity / mode have no equivalent, remote jobs with tracking need --trackio.space_id , and checkpoints are no longer uploaded as artifacts by default. FSDP1 is replaced by FSDP2/HSDP ( --parallelism.dp_shard , --parallelism.dp_replicate , --accelerator.* ); mixed precision is set with --accelerator.mixed_precision . FSDP checkpoints saved with lerobot ≤ 0.6.x cannot be resumed (their model.safetensors still loads), and Accelerate YAML/env configuration is rejected unless LEROBOT_ALLOW_ACCELERATE_ENV=1 . --policy.use_peft=true alone now trains LoRA instead of silently fully fine-tuning. Image transforms are batched: GaussianNoise , MotionBlur , GaussianPatchBrightness , RandomShadow , CoarseDropout , GammaCorrection and PlanckianJitter were silent no-ops on uint8 frames and now apply. ImageTransforms takes tensors only; the per-sample classes are deprecated. Inference & rollout lerobot.async_inference and lerobot[async] are removed: use lerobot[remote] , lerobot-policy-server and lerobot-rollout --inference.type=remote . lerobot.rollout.inference moved to lerobot.inference . select_action / predict_action_chunk may return a PolicyOutput ( {"action", "prediction"} ) instead of a bare tensor; use policy_output_to_transition …
